avoid sitting\u003cbr>continuously for many\u003cbr>hours\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduces vascular\u003cbr>stiffness, improves\u003cbr>glucose metabolism and\u003cbr>sympathetic balance\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Small but\u003cbr>meaningful BP\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Tell patient: “Even if you exercise,\u003cbr>prolonged sitting still worsens\u003cbr>cardiometabolic risk”\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Alcohol\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Men: max ≤2 drinks/day;\u003cbr>women: ≤1 drink/day;\u003cbr>ideally reduce/avoid if BP\u003cbr>uncontrolled\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Less sympathetic\u003cbr>activation, less weight\u003cbr>gain, better sleep, less\u003cbr>vasoconstriction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Around 4 mmHg\u003cbr>SBP reduction if\u003cbr>heavy drinker\u003cbr>reduces intake\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Binge drinking can trigger\u003cbr>hypertensive crisis, AF, stroke\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stop smoking\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Complete cessation\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduces acute\u003cbr>catecholamine surge,\u003cbr>endothelial injury, arterial\u003cbr>stiffness, thrombosis risk\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BP effect variable,\u003cbr>but major CV risk\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Smoking may not always cause\u003cbr>sustained clinic BP rise, but it\u003cbr>sharply increases MI/stroke risk\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stress\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meditation, breathing\u003cbr>control, yoga, sleep\u003cbr>optimization; When to start drugs\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In Tanzania/KCMC practical approach, start antihypertensive medication if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>BP persistently ≥140/90 mmHg\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>BP ≥160/100 mmHg: start treatment without delay\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Any BP with target-organ damage, diabetes, CKD, heart failure, stroke, or established\u003cbr>cardiovascular disease\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hypertensive emergency: admit and treat urgently with IV therapy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">WHO recommends starting pharmacological treatment no later than four weeks after confirmed\u003cbr>hypertension, but immediately if BP is high, such as ≥160/100 mmHg, or if there is end-organ\u003cbr>damage.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. First-line oral drugs commonly used in Tanzania/KCMC Common practical\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">first-line options:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Drug class\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Example\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Usual starting dose\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Calcium channel\u003cbr>blocker\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Amlodipine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>5 mg PO OD, increase to 10 mg OD\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>ACE inhibitor\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Enalapril\u003c/td>\u003ctd>5 mg PO OD/BD, titrate upward\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>ARB\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Losartan\u003c/td>\u003ctd>50 mg PO OD, increase to 100 mg\u003cbr>OD\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Thiazide diuretic\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hydrochlorothiazide\u003c/td>\u003ctd>12.5–25 mg PO OD\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Beta blocker\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Atenolol/Bisoprolol/Carvedilol\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Use when specific indication\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Beta blocker\u003cbr>Atenolol/Bisoprolol/Carvedilol  Use when specific indication\u003cbr>For many uncomplicated adult patients in Tanzania, amlodipine 5 mg once daily is a very\u003cbr>practical starting drug because it is available, effective, once daily, and does not require intensive\u003cbr>laboratory monitoring.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Stepwise drug escalation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: One drug if mild/moderate and low risk\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start with: Amlodipine 5 mg PO once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Review after 2–4 weeks. If BP is controlled, continue and reinforce lifestyle and adherence.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 13\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Add second drug if uncontrolled If\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">BP remains above target, add:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Losartan 50 mg PO once daily or\u003cbr>Enalapril 5 mg PO once/twice\u003cbr>daily A good practical\u003cbr>combination is: Amlodipine +\u003cbr>Losartan\u003cbr>or\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine + Enalapril\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not combine ACE inhibitor and ARB together.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Add thiazide diuretic If\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">still uncontrolled, add:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg PO once daily This\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">gives triple therapy:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CCB + ACEi/ARB + thiazide diuretic Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine 10 mg OD + Losartan 100 mg OD + Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: Resistant hypertension\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Resistant hypertension means BP remains uncontrolled despite 3 drugs, usually including a\u003cbr>diuretic, at appropriate doses.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before calling it resistant, check adherence, correct BP measurement, salt intake, NSAID use,\u003cbr>alcohol, CKD, OSA, and secondary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If true resistant hypertension, add:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Spironolactone 25 mg PO once daily Monitor\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">potassium and renal function.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Special Clinical Situations\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 14\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension with CKD or proteinuria\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use ACE inhibitor or ARB unless contraindicated because they reduce intraglomerular pressure\u003cbr>and proteinuria. Monitor creatinine and potassium after initiation. A mild creatinine rise is\u003cbr>acceptable, but severe rise or hyperkalemia requires reassessment.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension with heart failure\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If HFrEF, use guideline-directed therapy: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2\u003cbr>inhibitor, and diuretics for congestion. Avoid verapamil/diltiazem in HFrEF.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension with diabetes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACEi or ARB is preferred if albuminuria is present. Also control glucose, lipids, and  cardiovascular risk.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension in elderly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start low and go slow. Avoid sudden BP drops. Check postural BP. In elderly patients with\u003cbr>frailty, falls, or multiple comorbidities, targets may need individualization.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension in pregnancy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and spironolactone. Tanzania/MNH obstetric guidance commonly\u003cbr>uses methyldopa, nifedipine, and hydralazine depending on severity. For chronic hypertension in\u003cbr>pregnancy, methyldopa may start at 500 mg orally 8 hourly, with nifedipine added if BP remains\u003cbr>uncontrolled.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertensive Emergency\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertensive emergency is severe BP elevation with acute target-organ damage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hypertensive encephalopathy\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>acute stroke\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulmonary edema\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>acute coronary syndrome\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>aortic dissection\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>AKI\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>eclampsia/pre-eclampsia\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 15\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management is admission, ABCDE, cardiac monitoring, IV access, U&amp;E/creatinine, ECG,\u003cbr>fundoscopy, urinalysis, CXR if pulmonary edema, CT brain if neurological deficit, and IV\u003cbr>antihypertensive depending on indication.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid rapid uncontrolled BP drop except in aortic dissection. General target is to reduce MAP by\u003cbr>about 20–25% in the first hour, then gradually over 24–48 hours.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common IV options depending on availability:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Labetalol IV\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hydralazine IV\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Nitroglycerin IV for pulmonary edema/ACS\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Nicardipine IV where available\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Sodium nitroprusside in selected ICU settings\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In pregnancy-related severe hypertension/eclampsia, Tanzania job aid uses magnesium sulphate\u003cbr>for seizure control and hydralazine IV for severe BP control, with careful fluid balance.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">International Comparison — AHA/ACC 2025 and WHO\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The major difference is threshold and risk-based treatment intensity.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The AHA/ACC 2025 guideline uses ≥130/80 mmHg as the threshold for hypertension and\u003cbr>generally targets &lt;130/80 mmHg in most adults, with individualized exceptions. It also\u003cbr>recommends using cardiovascular risk assessments, such as PREVENT, to decide when to start\u003cbr>medication in lower-risk stage 1 hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The WHO 2021 guideline is more pragmatic for many health systems: it recommends drug\u003cbr>treatment for confirmed BP ≥140/90 mmHg, and for SBP 130–139 mmHg when there is\u003cbr>established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD, or high cardiovascular risk. WHO\u003cbr>recommends first-line therapy from three main classes: thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics,\u003cbr>ACEi/ARB, and long-acting dihydropyridine CCBs.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tanzania/KCMC practice is closer to the WHO public-health model: confirm hypertension, start\u003cbr>affordable available drugs, often amlodipine-based treatment, add ACEi/ARB and thiazide as\u003cbr>needed, and focus heavily on adherence and follow-up.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Follow-Up\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Review newly treated patients after 2–4 weeks. Check BP, side effects, adherence, lifestyle, and\u003cbr>complications. Check creatinine and potassium after ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, or diuretic\u003cbr>initiation/escalation.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 16\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Once controlled, follow every 1–3 months initially, then every 3–6 months depending on risk  and stability.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>"}],"words":2571,"searchtext":" hypertension definition hypertension is a chronic elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure. in most adult clinical settings, hypertension is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure readings are ≥140/90 mmhg, while the 2025 aha/acc guideline defines high blood pressure from ≥130/80 mmhg and recommends treatment targets generally below 130/80 mmhg for most adults. in tanzania/kcmc practice, diagnosis and treatment often follow the practical public-health threshold of bp ≥140/90 mmhg, consistent with who and tanzania stg approaches. who recommends starting pharmacological treatment for confirmed hypertension at sbp ≥140 mmhg or dbp ≥90 mmhg, and earlier treatment at sbp 130–139 mmhg if the patient has cardiovascular disease, diabetes, ckd, or high cardiovascular risk. classification category bp level normal \u003c120/\u003c80 mmhg elevated / high-normal 120–129/\u003c80 mmhg stage 1 hypertension 130–139 or 80–89 mmhg stage 2 hypertension ≥140 or ≥90 mmhg severe hypertension ≥180 and/or ≥120 mmhg in ward work, always separate uncomplicated hypertension from hypertensive emergency. hypertensive emergency means severe bp elevation with acute target-organ damage, such as stroke, pulmonary edema, acs, aki, aortic dissection, encephalopathy, or eclampsia. risk factors common risk factors include age, obesity, high salt intake, alcohol use, smoking, physical inactivity, diabetes, ckd, dyslipidemia, family history, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic nsaid/steroid use. in tanzania, also think of poor treatment adherence, late diagnosis, limited home bp monitoring, high dietary salt, alcohol, obesity, ckd, and secondary causes in young patients. clinical features most patients are asymptomatic. symptoms, when present, may include headache, dizziness, palpitations, visual symptoms, chest pain, dyspnea, or features of complications. look specifically for target-organ damage: lvh/heart failure, stroke/tia, ckd/proteinuria, hypertensive retinopathy, peripheral vascular disease, and coronary artery disease. diagnostic evaluation confirm bp properly using correct cuff size, patient seated and rested, arm supported, and repeated measurements. diagnosis should not be made from one reading unless there is hypertensive emergency. proper bp measurement — diagnostic evaluation accurate bp measurement is part of diagnosis. a wrong position, wrong cuff, talking, full bladder, or measuring immediately after walking can falsely raise bp and may lead to overdiagnosis or unnecessary treatment. aha guidance emphasizes seated, rested, quiet measurement with the arm supported at heart level, feet flat, and cuff on bare skin. 1. before measuring bp the patient should avoid the following for at least 30 minutes before measurement: avoid before bp why caffeine/coffee/energy drinks can transiently raise bp smoking/nicotine sympathetic stimulation raises bp exercise/walking fast raises bp temporarily full bladder can falsely elevate bp talking/phone use can falsely elevate reading before taking bp, ask the patient to sit quietly and rest for at least 5 minutes. aha home bp instructions specifically advise no caffeine, smoking, or exercise within 30 minutes, emptying the bladder, and resting quietly for 5 minutes before measurement. 2. correct patient position body part correct position why it matters back supported against chair unsupported back can falsely raise bp feet flat on floor dangling feet can increase bp legs uncrossed crossed legs can falsely increase bp arm supported on table unsupported arm can falsely raise bp cuff level mid-arm at heart level arm below heart level overestimates bp cuff placement bare upper arm, not over clothes clothes interfere with cuff compression patient silent and still talking can raise bp significantly aha notes that the patient should sit upright with back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, and arm supported at heart level. cdc gives the same core steps: no talking, cuff on bare skin, back supported, feet flat, and arm at chest/heart height. 3. correct cuff size and placement use an appropriate cuff based on mid-arm circumference. the inflatable bladder should cover most of the upper arm circumference and length. a cuff that is too small gives falsely high bp; a cuff that is too large may give falsely low bp. place the cuff on the bare upper arm, about 2–3 cm above the antecubital fossa, with the artery marker over the brachial artery. the arm should be relaxed and supported at heart level. 4. how many readings to take in clinic do not diagnose hypertension from one casual reading unless the patient has hypertensive emergency with acute target-organ damage. for routine clinic diagnosis: step what to do first visit measure bp in both arms if different use the arm with the higher reading for future measurements during each visit take at least 2 readings, 1 minute apart if readings differ take a third reading significantly diagnosis use the average of repeated readings over at least 2 separate visits aha/acc guidance emphasizes accurate measurement and repeated readings; clinical practice guidelines recommend repeating bp measurements on two or more occasions before diagnosing hypertension. 5. first visit: measure both arms at the first assessment, bp should be measured in both arms. if one arm is consistently higher, document it and use that arm for future readings. a persistent inter-arm difference may suggest: • peripheral arterial disease, • subclavian stenosis, • aortic disease, • vascular obstruction. 6. standing bp: when to check postural bp measure lying/sitting and standing bp in patients at risk of orthostatic hypotension, especially: • elderly patients, • diabetes, • autonomic neuropathy, • parkinsonism, • recurrent dizziness/falls, • dehydration, • patients on diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates, or multiple antihypertensives. how to do it: 1. measure bp after lying or sitting for 5 minutes. 2. ask patient to stand. 3. measure bp at 1 minute and 3 minutes after standing. orthostatic hypotension is suggested by: • fall in sbp ≥20 mmhg, or • fall in dbp ≥10 mmhg, within 3 minutes of standing. 7. home bp monitoring home bp is useful to confirm diagnosis, detect white-coat hypertension, detect masked hypertension, and improve follow-up. correct home bp method: timing what patient does morning measure before breakfast and before bp medicines evening measure before supper/bed each sitting take 2 readings, 1 minute apart duration do this for 3–7 days interpretation average the readings, excluding day 1 if possible the american heart association advises being still, resting for at least 5 minutes before measuring, avoiding talking, using a cuff on bare skin, and taking measurements correctly at home. 8. ambulatory bp monitoring ambulatory bp monitoring is the best method when available. it is useful for: • suspected white-coat hypertension, • suspected masked hypertension, • resistant hypertension, • episodic hypertension, • hypotensive symptoms on treatment, • pregnancy hypertension assessment where available. it records bp over 24 hours and gives daytime, nighttime, and average bp. baseline investigations should include fbp, serum creatinine/egfr, urea, sodium, potassium, fasting/random glucose or hba1c, lipid profile, urinalysis or urine acr, ecg, and fundoscopy where available. do echocardiography if there is suspected hypertensive heart disease, heart failure, murmur, or lvh. in young patients, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, renal bruit, abrupt onset, or severe hypertension, evaluate for secondary hypertension. management — tanzania practical regime first 1. lifestyle modification for all patients all hypertensive patients need lifestyle treatment, whether or not drugs are started. advise salt reduction, weight reduction, regular aerobic better monitoring as part of modern bp record readings control care 2. when to start drugs in tanzania/kcmc practical approach, start antihypertensive medication if: • bp persistently ≥140/90 mmhg • bp ≥160/100 mmhg: start treatment without delay • any bp with target-organ damage, diabetes, ckd, heart failure, stroke, or established cardiovascular disease • hypertensive emergency: admit and treat urgently with iv therapy who recommends starting pharmacological treatment no later than four weeks after confirmed hypertension, but immediately if bp is high, such as ≥160/100 mmhg, or if there is end-organ damage. 3. first-line oral drugs commonly used in tanzania/kcmc common practical first-line options: drug class example usual starting dose calcium channel amlodipine 5 mg po od, increase to 10 mg od blocker ace inhibitor enalapril 5 mg po od/bd, titrate upward arb losartan 50 mg po od, increase to 100 mg od thiazide diuretic hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po od beta blocker atenolol/bisoprolol/carvedilol use when specific indication for many uncomplicated adult patients in tanzania, amlodipine 5 mg once daily is a very practical starting drug because it is available, effective, once daily, and does not require intensive laboratory monitoring. 4. stepwise drug escalation step 1: one drug if mild/moderate and low risk start with: amlodipine 5 mg po once daily review after 2–4 weeks. if bp is controlled, continue and reinforce lifestyle and adherence. step 2: add second drug if uncontrolled if bp remains above target, add: losartan 50 mg po once daily or enalapril 5 mg po once/twice daily a good practical combination is: amlodipine + losartan or amlodipine + enalapril do not combine ace inhibitor and arb together. step 3: add thiazide diuretic if still uncontrolled, add: hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po once daily this gives triple therapy: ccb + acei/arb + thiazide diuretic example: amlodipine 10 mg od + losartan 100 mg od + hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg od step 4: resistant hypertension resistant hypertension means bp remains uncontrolled despite 3 drugs, usually including a diuretic, at appropriate doses. before calling it resistant, check adherence, correct bp measurement, salt intake, nsaid use, alcohol, ckd, osa, and secondary hypertension. if true resistant hypertension, add: spironolactone 25 mg po once daily monitor potassium and renal function. special clinical situations hypertension with ckd or proteinuria use ace inhibitor or arb unless contraindicated because they reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. monitor creatinine and potassium after initiation. a mild creatinine rise is acceptable, but severe rise or hyperkalemia requires reassessment. hypertension with heart failure if hfref, use guideline-directed therapy: acei/arb/arni, beta blocker, mra, sglt2 inhibitor, and diuretics for congestion. avoid verapamil/diltiazem in hfref. hypertension with diabetes acei or arb is preferred if albuminuria is present. also control glucose, lipids, and cardiovascular risk. hypertension in elderly start low and go slow. avoid sudden bp drops. check postural bp. in elderly patients with frailty, falls, or multiple comorbidities, targets may need individualization. hypertension in pregnancy avoid ace inhibitors, arbs, and spironolactone. tanzania/mnh obstetric guidance commonly uses methyldopa, nifedipine, and hydralazine depending on severity. for chronic hypertension in pregnancy, methyldopa may start at 500 mg orally 8 hourly, with nifedipine added if bp remains uncontrolled. hypertensive emergency hypertensive emergency is severe bp elevation with acute target-organ damage. examples include: • hypertensive encephalopathy • acute stroke • pulmonary edema • acute coronary syndrome • aortic dissection • aki • eclampsia/pre-eclampsia management is admission, abcde, cardiac monitoring, iv access, u&e/creatinine, ecg, fundoscopy, urinalysis, cxr if pulmonary edema, ct brain if neurological deficit, and iv antihypertensive depending on indication. avoid rapid uncontrolled bp drop except in aortic dissection. general target is to reduce map by about 20–25% in the first hour, then gradually over 24–48 hours. common iv options depending on availability: • labetalol iv • hydralazine iv • nitroglycerin iv for pulmonary edema/acs • nicardipine iv where available • sodium nitroprusside in selected icu settings in pregnancy-related severe hypertension/eclampsia, tanzania job aid uses magnesium sulphate for seizure control and hydralazine iv for severe bp control, with careful fluid balance. international comparison — aha/acc 2025 and who the major difference is threshold and risk-based treatment intensity. the aha/acc 2025 guideline uses ≥130/80 mmhg as the threshold for hypertension and generally targets \u003c130/80 mmhg in most adults, with individualized exceptions. it also recommends using cardiovascular risk assessments, such as prevent, to decide when to start medication in lower-risk stage 1 hypertension. the who 2021 guideline is more pragmatic for many health systems: it recommends drug treatment for confirmed bp ≥140/90 mmhg, and for sbp 130–139 mmhg when there is established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, ckd, or high cardiovascular risk. who recommends first-line therapy from three main classes: thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics, acei/arb, and long-acting dihydropyridine ccbs. tanzania/kcmc practice is closer to the who public-health model: confirm hypertension, start affordable available drugs, often amlodipine-based treatment, add acei/arb and thiazide as needed, and focus heavily on adherence and follow-up. follow-up review newly treated patients after 2–4 weeks. check bp, side effects, adherence, lifestyle, and complications. check creatinine and potassium after acei/arb, spironolactone, or diuretic initiation/escalation. once controlled, follow every 1–3 months initially, then every 3–6 months depending on 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">HYPERTENSION\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension is a chronic elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure. In most adult clinical\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">settings, hypertension is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure readings are ≥140/90 mmHg,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">while the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline defines high blood pressure from ≥130/80 mmHg and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">recommends treatment targets generally below 130/80 mmHg for most adults.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In Tanzania/KCMC practice, diagnosis and treatment often follow the practical public-health\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">threshold of BP ≥140/90 mmHg, consistent with WHO and Tanzania STG approaches. WHO\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">recommends starting pharmacological treatment for confirmed hypertension at SBP ≥140 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">or DBP ≥90 mmHg, and earlier treatment at SBP 130–139 mmHg if the patient has\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD, or high cardiovascular risk.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Classification\u003c/h4>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Category\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BP level\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Normal\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&lt;120/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Elevated / high-normal\u003c/td>\u003ctd>120–129/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stage 1 hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>130–139 or 80–89 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stage 2 hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥140 or ≥90 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Severe hypertension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥180 and/or ≥120 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In ward work, always separate uncomplicated hypertension from hypertensive emergency.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertensive emergency means severe BP elevation with acute target-organ damage, such as\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">stroke, pulmonary edema, ACS, AKI, aortic dissection, encephalopathy, or eclampsia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The key clinical point is that hypertensive crisis must be divided into:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Hypertensive urgency — severe BP elevation without acute target-organ damage.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Hypertensive emergency — severe BP elevation with acute target-organ damage.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Diagnostic Evaluation Before Treatment\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Confirm BP properly using correct cuff size, patient seated, back supported, feet flat, arm\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">supported at heart level, and after at least 5 minutes rest. Take at least 2 readings, 1 minute apart,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and use the average. Diagnosis should not be made from one isolated reading unless there is\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hypertensive emergency.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Baseline investigations should include FBP, serum creatinine/eGFR, urea, sodium, potassium,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">fasting/random glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile, urinalysis or urine ACR, ECG, and fundoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">where available. The 2025 AHA/ACC update emphasizes urine albumin/creatinine testing for\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">newly diagnosed hypertension to detect early kidney injury and refine cardiovascular/renal risk.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do echocardiography if there is suspected hypertensive heart disease, heart failure, murmur,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">LVH, or pulmonary hypertension. In young patients, resistant hypertension, abrupt onset,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hypokalemia, renal bruit, severe hypertension, or worsening renal function, evaluate for\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">secondary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Management by BP Stage\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Normal BP: &lt;120/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">No antihypertensive medication is needed. Advise maintenance of healthy lifestyle: normal\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">weight, regular physical activity, low-salt diet, DASH-style diet, avoid smoking, limit alcohol,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and periodic BP screening.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Elevated BP: 120–129/&lt;80 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management is lifestyle modification only. This includes salt reduction, weight control,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">exercise, DASH diet, alcohol reduction, smoking cessation, adequate sleep, and home BP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">monitoring.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Recheck BP in 3–6 months, or earlier if the patient has high cardiovascular risk.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 or 80–89 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If BP is 130–139/80–89 and the patient have no diabetes, CKD, CVD, or target-organ damage,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">we usually emphasize lifestyle modification and close follow-up rather than immediate drugs.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start medication if the patient has: diabetes mellitus, CKD, stroke/TIA, ischemic heart disease,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">heart failure, albuminuria, LVH, high cardiovascular risk, persistent BP despite lifestyle\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">modification.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">2025 AHA/ACC approach\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AHA/ACC recommends treatment based on BP stage plus cardiovascular risk. For low-risk\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Stage 1 hypertension, lifestyle modification is first, with reassessment after 3–6 months. If BP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">remains above target, medication is added. For Stage 1 hypertension with diabetes, CKD,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">established cardiovascular disease, or high risk, start lifestyle plus medication early.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Stage 2 Hypertension: ≥140 or ≥90 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This usually requires lifestyle modification plus medication.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tanzania/KCMC practical starting regimen Common\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">first-line oral options:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Amlodipine 5 mg PO once daily Calcium channel blocker Increase\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">to 10 mg once daily if needed.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. If not controlled, add Losartan 50 mg PO once daily ARB Increase\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">to 100 mg once daily if needed.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. If still uncontrolled, add Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg PO\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">once daily. Thiazide diuretic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A practical triple regimen is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine 10 mg OD + Losartan 100 mg OD + Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Alternative ACE inhibitor: Enalapril 5 mg PO once or twice daily, titrated upward depending\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">on BP, creatinine, and potassium.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid ACEi/ARB in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, significant AKI, and severe\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hyperkalemia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">STEPWISE DRUG ESCALATION\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: One drug if mild/moderate and low risk CCB\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start with: Amlodipine 5 mg PO once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Review after 2–4 weeks. If BP is controlled, continue and reinforce lifestyle and adherence.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Add second drug if uncontrolled If BP remains above target, add: ACE/ARB\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Losartan 50 mg PO once daily or   Enalapril 5 mg PO once/twice daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A good practical combination is:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine + Losartan\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">or\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine + Enalapril\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not combine ACE inhibitor and ARB together. Step\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">3: Add thiazide diuretic THIAZIDE DIURETIC\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If still uncontrolled, add:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg PO once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This gives triple therapy:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CCB + ACEi/ARB + thiazide diuretic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Amlodipine 10 mg OD + Losartan 100 mg OD + Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: Resistant hypertension POTASSIUM SPARING DIURETIC\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Resistant hypertension means BP remains uncontrolled despite 3 drugs, usually including a\u003cbr>diuretic, at appropriate doses.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before calling it resistant, check adherence, correct BP measurement, salt intake, NSAID use,\u003cbr>alcohol, CKD, OSA, and secondary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If true resistant hypertension, add:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Spironolactone 25 mg PO once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Monitor potassium and renal function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">2025 AHA/ACC approach\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For Stage 2 hypertension, especially if BP is ≥20/10 mmHg above target, AHA/ACC favors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">starting two first-line drugs, preferably as a single-pill combination where available, to improve\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">adherence and reach target faster. First-line drug classes remain thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACEi/ARB, and long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Lifestyle Modification for All Patients\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Lifestyle modification is required whether or not drugs are started. Use:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. sodium restriction: ideally ≤1500 mg/day, or at least reduce by 1000 mg/day,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. weight loss if overweight: approximately 1 mmHg SBP reduction per 1 kg lost,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. DASH-style diet,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. aerobic exercise: 150 minutes/week, for example 30 minutes/day for 5 days,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. resistance training 2–3 days/week,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. reduce sitting time; break sitting every 30–60 minutes,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. limit alcohol,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. stop smoking,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">9. sleep 7–9 hours/night,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">10. avoid NSAIDs where possible,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">11. home BP monitoring.\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>LIFESTYLE\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>RECOMMENDED\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>HOW IT\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>EXPECTED\u003c/td>\u003ctd>CLINICAL NOTE\u003c/td>\u003ctd>CLINICAL NOTE\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>INTERVENTION\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>LIMIT / TARGET\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>LOWERS BP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BP BENEFIT\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Salt / sodium\u003cbr>restriction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Aim for ≤1,500 mg\u003cbr>sodium/day if\u003cbr>possible; at least\u003cbr>reduce by 1,000\u003cbr>mg/day from usual\u003cbr>intake\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Less sodium →\u003cbr>less water\u003cbr>retention →\u003cbr>reduced\u003cbr>intravascular\u003cbr>volume and\u003cbr>arterial stiffness\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>About 5–6\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>reduction;\u003cbr>more in\u003cbr>saltsensitive\u003cbr>patients\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Very important in elderly,\u003cbr>Black patients, CKD, HF,\u003cbr>and resistant HTN. Avoid\u003cbr>adding salt at table;\u003cbr>reduce processed foods,\u003cbr>salted snacks, canned\u003cbr>foods, and stock cubes\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Weight loss\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>If overweight/obese:\u003cbr>aim for ≥5% body\u003cbr>weight loss initially;\u003cbr>long-term BMI\u003cbr>around 18.5–24.9\u003cbr>kg/m²\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduces\u003cbr>sympathetic\u003cbr>tone, insulin\u003cbr>resistance,\u003cbr>RAAS\u003cbr>activation, sleep\u003cbr>apnea burden,\u003cbr>and vascular\u003cbr>resistance\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>About 1\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>per 1 kg\u003cbr>weight loss\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Even 5–10 kg loss can\u003cbr>significantly reduce BP\u003cbr>and drug requirement\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>DASH diet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Daily\u003cbr>fruits/vegetables,\u003cbr>whole grains,\u003cbr>legumes, low-fat\u003cbr>dairy; reduce\u003cbr>saturated fat, red\u003cbr>meat, sugary foods\u003c/td>\u003ctd>High potassium,\u003cbr>magnesium,\u003cbr>calcium, fiber;\u003cbr>improves\u003cbr>endothelial\u003cbr>function and\u003cbr>natriuresis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Around 8–11\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>reduction in\u003cbr>hypertensive\u003cbr>patients\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Best diet pattern for\u003cbr>hypertension. Works even\u003cbr>better when\u003cbr>combined with sodium\u003cbr>restriction\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Potassium intake\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Increase dietary\u003cbr>potassium through\u003cbr>fruits/vegetables\u003cbr>unless\u003cbr>contraindicated\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Potassium\u003cbr>increases sodium\u003cbr>excretion,\u003cbr>relaxes vessels,\u003cbr>and reduces\u003cbr>vascular tone\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Around 4–5\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Avoid high potassium\u003cbr>advice in CKD,\u003cbr>hyperkalemia,\u003cbr>ACEi/ARB/MRA users\u003cbr>unless potassium is\u003cbr>monitored\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Aerobic exercise\u003c/td>\u003ctd>At least 150\u003cbr>min/week moderate\u003cbr>intensity, e.g. brisk\u003cbr>walking 30 min/day,\u003cbr>5 days/week\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Improves\u003cbr>vascular\u003cbr>compliance,\u003cbr>insulin\u003cbr>sensitivity,\u003cbr>weight,\u003cbr>endothelial nitric\u003cbr>oxide, and\u003cbr>sympathetic\u003cbr>balance\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Around 5–8\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Brisk walking is enough.\u003cbr>Patient should be able to\u003cbr>talk but not sing during\u003cbr>exercise\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Resistance exercise\u003c/td>\u003ctd>2–3 days/week\u003cbr>muscle-\u003cbr>strengthening\u003cbr>exercises\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Improves\u003cbr>vascular\u003cbr>function, muscle\u003cbr>glucose uptake,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Around 3–5\u003cbr>mmHg SBP\u003cbr>reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Combine with aerobic\u003cbr>exercise. Avoid\u003cbr>breathholding/Valsalva in\u003cbr>uncontrolled severe HTN\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>and metabolic\u003cbr>profile\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Reduce sedentary\u003cbr>time\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Break sitting every\u003cbr>30–60 minutes;\u003cbr>avoid sitting\u003cbr>continuously for\u003cbr>many hours\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduces\u003cbr>vascular\u003cbr>stiffness,\u003cbr>improves\u003cbr>glucose\u003cbr>metabolism and\u003cbr>sympathetic\u003cbr>balance\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Small but\u003cbr>meaningful\u003cbr>BP reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Tell patient: “Even if you\u003cbr>exercise, prolonged\u003cbr>sitting still worsens\u003cbr>cardiometabolic risk”\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Alcohol reduction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Men: max ≤2\u003cbr>drinks/day; In Tanzanian obstetric emergency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">guidance, hydralazine is started when\u003cbr>DBP is ≥110 mmHg, with hydralazine\u003cbr>10 mg IV slowly every 30 minutes\u003cbr>until DBP falls to about 100 mmHg.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hydralazine is useful but less predictable than labetalol or nicardipine. arterial blood pressure. in most adult clinical settings, hypertension is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure readings are ≥140/90 mmhg, while the 2025 aha/acc guideline defines high blood pressure from ≥130/80 mmhg and recommends treatment targets generally below 130/80 mmhg for most adults. in tanzania/kcmc practice, diagnosis and treatment often follow the practical public-health threshold of bp ≥140/90 mmhg, consistent with who and tanzania stg approaches. who recommends starting pharmacological treatment for confirmed hypertension at sbp ≥140 mmhg or dbp ≥90 mmhg, and earlier treatment at sbp 130–139 mmhg if the patient has cardiovascular disease, diabetes, ckd, or high cardiovascular risk. classification category bp level normal \u003c120/\u003c80 mmhg elevated / high-normal 120–129/\u003c80 mmhg stage 1 hypertension 130–139 or 80–89 mmhg stage 2 hypertension ≥140 or ≥90 mmhg severe hypertension ≥180 and/or ≥120 mmhg in ward work, always separate uncomplicated hypertension from hypertensive emergency. hypertensive emergency means severe bp elevation with acute target-organ damage, such as stroke, pulmonary edema, acs, aki, aortic dissection, encephalopathy, or eclampsia. the key clinical point is that hypertensive crisis must be divided into: 1. hypertensive urgency — severe bp elevation without acute target-organ damage. 2. hypertensive emergency — severe bp elevation with acute target-organ damage. 2. diagnostic evaluation before treatment confirm bp properly using correct cuff size, patient seated, back supported, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, and after at least 5 minutes rest. take at least 2 readings, 1 minute apart, and use the average. diagnosis should not be made from one isolated reading unless there is hypertensive emergency. baseline investigations should include fbp, serum creatinine/egfr, urea, sodium, potassium, fasting/random glucose or hba1c, lipid profile, urinalysis or urine acr, ecg, and fundoscopy where available. the 2025 aha/acc update emphasizes urine albumin/creatinine testing for newly diagnosed hypertension to detect early kidney injury and refine cardiovascular/renal risk. do echocardiography if there is suspected hypertensive heart disease, heart failure, murmur, lvh, or pulmonary hypertension. in young patients, resistant hypertension, abrupt onset, hypokalemia, renal bruit, severe hypertension, or worsening renal function, evaluate for secondary hypertension. 3. management by bp stage a. normal bp: \u003c120/\u003c80 mmhg no antihypertensive medication is needed. advise maintenance of healthy lifestyle: normal weight, regular physical activity, low-salt diet, dash-style diet, avoid smoking, limit alcohol, and periodic bp screening. b. elevated bp: 120–129/\u003c80 mmhg management is lifestyle modification only. this includes salt reduction, weight control, exercise, dash diet, alcohol reduction, smoking cessation, adequate sleep, and home bp monitoring. recheck bp in 3–6 months, or earlier if the patient has high cardiovascular risk. c. stage 1 hypertension: 130–139 or 80–89 mmhg if bp is 130–139/80–89 and the patient have no diabetes, ckd, cvd, or target-organ damage, we usually emphasize lifestyle modification and close follow-up rather than immediate drugs. start medication if the patient has: diabetes mellitus, ckd, stroke/tia, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, albuminuria, lvh, high cardiovascular risk, persistent bp despite lifestyle modification. 2025 aha/acc approach aha/acc recommends treatment based on bp stage plus cardiovascular risk. for low-risk stage 1 hypertension, lifestyle modification is first, with reassessment after 3–6 months. if bp remains above target, medication is added. for stage 1 hypertension with diabetes, ckd, established cardiovascular disease, or high risk, start lifestyle plus medication early. d. stage 2 hypertension: ≥140 or ≥90 mmhg this usually requires lifestyle modification plus medication. tanzania/kcmc practical starting regimen common first-line oral options: 1. amlodipine 5 mg po once daily calcium channel blocker increase to 10 mg once daily if needed. 2. if not controlled, add losartan 50 mg po once daily arb increase to 100 mg once daily if needed. 3. if still uncontrolled, add hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po once daily. thiazide diuretic a practical triple regimen is: amlodipine 10 mg od + losartan 100 mg od + hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg od alternative ace inhibitor: enalapril 5 mg po once or twice daily, titrated upward depending on bp, creatinine, and potassium. avoid acei/arb in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, significant aki, and severe hyperkalemia. stepwise drug escalation step 1: one drug if mild/moderate and low risk ccb start with: amlodipine 5 mg po once daily review after 2–4 weeks. if bp is controlled, continue and reinforce lifestyle and adherence. step 2: add second drug if uncontrolled if bp remains above target, add: ace/arb losartan 50 mg po once daily or enalapril 5 mg po once/twice daily a good practical combination is: amlodipine + losartan or amlodipine + enalapril do not combine ace inhibitor and arb together. step 3: add thiazide diuretic thiazide diuretic if still uncontrolled, add: hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po once daily this gives triple therapy: ccb + acei/arb + thiazide diuretic example: amlodipine 10 mg od + losartan 100 mg od + hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg od step 4: resistant hypertension potassium sparing diuretic resistant hypertension means bp remains uncontrolled despite 3 drugs, usually including a diuretic, at appropriate doses. before calling it resistant, check adherence, correct bp measurement, salt intake, nsaid use, alcohol, ckd, osa, and secondary hypertension. if true resistant hypertension, add: spironolactone 25 mg po once daily monitor potassium and renal function. 2025 aha/acc approach for stage 2 hypertension, especially if bp is ≥20/10 mmhg above target, aha/acc favors starting two first-line drugs, preferably as a single-pill combination where available, to improve adherence and reach target faster. first-line drug classes remain thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics, acei/arb, and long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. 4. lifestyle modification for all patients lifestyle modification is required whether or not drugs are started. use: 1. sodium restriction: ideally ≤1500 mg/day, or at least reduce by 1000 mg/day, 2. weight loss if overweight: approximately 1 mmhg sbp reduction per 1 kg lost, 3. dash-style diet, 4. aerobic exercise: 150 minutes/week, for example 30 minutes/day for 5 days, 5. resistance training 2–3 days/week, 6. reduce sitting time; break sitting every 30–60 minutes, 7. limit alcohol, 8. stop smoking, 9. sleep 7–9 hours/night, 10. avoid nsaids where possible, 11. home bp monitoring. lifestyle recommended how it expected clinical note intervention limit / target titration control hypertensive urgency hypertensive urgency is severe bp elevation, usually ≥180/120 mmhg, but without acute target-organ damage. management of hypertensive urgency 1. start with abc assessment but patients are usually stable assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurological status, chest pain, dyspnea, urine output, and visual symptoms to exclude emergencies. if there is no target-organ damage, this is not an ivdrug situation. 2. let the patient rest and repeat bp allow the patient to rest quietly for 30 minutes, then repeat bp using proper technique. sometimes bp falls after rest, pain control, and anxiety reduction. 3. do basic investigations if available do: creatinine/egfr , electrolytes, urinalysis ,ecg , glucose and fundoscopy if possible this helps exclude silent target-organ damage. 4. use oral antihypertensive treatment do not rapidly drop bp. in practical setting, oral options include: amlodipine 1. amlodipine 5–10 mg po once daily good for most uncomplicated patients. nifedipine retard / long acting nifedipine 2. nifedipine retard 20 mg po 12 hourly or long- acting formulation depending on availability. avoid short-acting sublingual nifedipine because it can cause sudden uncontrolled hypotension, stroke, or myocardial ischemia. losartan 3. losartan 50 mg po once daily increase to 100 mg once daily . if needed. avoid in pregnancy and caution in aki/hyperkalemia. enalapril 4. enalapril 5 mg po once or twice daily titrate upward depending on bp, renal function, and potassium. avoid pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, aki, or hyperkalemia. hydrochlorothiazide 5. hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg po once daily useful especially in salt-sensitive hypertension. follow-up for hypertensive urgency, follow up should be close: 1. review within 24–72 hours if bp very high or high risk 2. otherwise within 1 week 3. adjust medications gradually 4. assess adherence and side effects 5. education warning signs the goal is gradual reduction over days to weeks, not minutes to hours. hypertensive emergency a practical approach is: if iv labetalol is available give: 1. labetalol 20 mg iv slowly over 2 minutes then repeat: 2. 40 mg iv after 10 minutes if bp remains high then: 3. 80 mg iv every 10 minutes as needed maximum total dose: 300 mg alternatively, use infusion if available. avoid or use caution in: severe asthma/copd with bronchospasm bradycardia heart block acute decompensated heart failure/pulmonary edema if labetalol is not available, or in many tanzania settings use: 4. hydralazine 5–10 mg iv slowly repeat every: 5. 20–30 minutes until target bp reduction is achieved. 6. in tanzanian obstetric emergency guidance, hydralazine is started when dbp is ≥110 mmhg, with hydralazine 10 mg iv slowly every 30 minutes until dbp falls to about 100 mmhg. hydralazine is useful but less predictable than labetalol or nicardipine. it may cause: reflex tachycardia headache flushing excessive bp drop so monitor bp closely. if acute pulmonary edema is present this is a hypertensive emergency with heart failure. management: 1. sit patient upright 2. oxygen if hypoxic 3. niv/cpap if severe respiratory distress 4. iv furosemide 40–80 mg stat, then reassess 5. iv nitroglycerin infusion if available and sbp allows avoid aggressive beta-blockers in acute pulmonary edema because they may worsen acute decompensated heart failure. if aortic dissection is suspected; this is the exception where bp and heart rate must be reduced rapidly. target: sbp \u003c120 mmhg hr around 60 bpm start with beta-blockade first: iv labetalol or iv esmolol. then add vasodilator if bp remains high. do not give vasodilator alone before beta-blocker because reflex tachycardia can worsen aortic shear stress. if stroke is suspected acute ischemic stroke if not receiving thrombolysis, do not lower bp unless very high, commonly >220/120 mmhg, unless there is another emergency such as aortic dissection or pulmonary edema. if eligible for thrombolysis, bp must be lowered to \u003c185/110 mmhg before alteplase and maintained \u003c180/105 mmhg after thrombolysis. intracerebral hemorrhage bp is lowered more actively than ischemic stroke but still controlled. avoid sudden large drops. iv labetalol or nicardipine is commonly used."},{"id":"pdf-8","disease":"Upper GI
